title: Lærdal Tunnel
content: # Lærdal Tunnel. The **Lærdal Tunnel** (Norwegian: *Lærdalstunnelen*) is a 24.51-kilometre-long (15.23 mi) road tunnel connecting Lærdal Municipality and Aurland Municipality in Vestland county, Norway; the southwest end of the tunnel is approximately 117 kilometres (73 mi) northeast of Bergen "Bergen (city)"). In 1992, Parliament confirmed that decision, added that the road should run through a tunnel between Lærdal Municipality and Aurland Municipality, and passed legislation to build the tunnel. The tunnel begins just east of Aurlandsvangen in Aurland Municipality, goes under a mountain range, and ends 5.5 kilometres (3.4 mi) south of Lærdalsøyri in Lærdal Municipality. Its design takes into consideration the mental strain of driving through a long tunnel; it is divided into four sections, separated by three large mountain caves (with parking areas available) at 6-kilometre (3.7 mi) intervals. The Lærdal Tunnel is the first in the world to be equipped with an air treatment plant, located in a 100-metre (330 ft)-wide cavern about 9.5 kilometres (5.9 mi) northwest of Aurlandsvangen.

title: The Lærdal Tunnel - Nordge
content: # Sunrise and Northern Lights in the Lærdal Tunnel. Lærdalstunnelen is the world's longest road tunnel, 24,5 km long, connecting Lærdal to Aurland in Sogn og Fjordane county in western Norway, on the road linking Oslo to Bergen. During a trip in 2018, we used it twice: first to explore the region, Flåm, the fjord, and the Stegastein footbridge; and second to visit our colleague at the hospital in Bergen. The tunnel is divided into four sections separated by three large caverns carved into the mountain, which break up the monotony, providing a soothing and luminous view reminiscent of the Northern Lights, and allowing for U-turns. While the main tunnel is lit white, the caves are illuminated blue with yellow lights around the perimeter to create the illusion of a sunrise or the Northern Lights. The Lærdal Tunnel is the first in the world to be equipped with an air treatment plant, located in a cavern 100 meters wide.

title: E16 Lærdal Tunnel | Statens vegvesen
content: The tunnel is the longest road tunnel in the world, and it will now be upgraded to meet today's safety requirements. Since 2015, the Norwegian Public Roads Administration (NPRA) has upgraded national road tunnels throughout the country. The goal is to meet the requirements of the Tunnel Safety Regulations. The NPRA issued an invitation to tender for the contract to upgrade the world's longest road tunnel in October 2025. Upgrading of the E16 Lærdal Tunnel will start in the autumn of 2026. Once the heaviest work with blasting and securing has been completed, it will be possible to allow a little more traffic through the tunnel, even though work will be going on at night. The Lærdal Tunnel is the world's longest road tunnel with a length of 24,509 metres. An invitation to tender for the tunnel upgrade project was issued in the autumn of 2025, and the work is scheduled to start in the autumn of 2026.
